text:
PRADHAN MANTRI UCHCHATAR SHIKSHA PROTSAHAN (PM-USP) YOJANA

GUIDELINES FOR THE COMPONENT SCHEME –
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEME OF SCHOLARSHIP FOR COLLEGE AND
UNIVERSITY STUDENTS (PM-USP CSSS)

(Applicable for academic year 2022-23 onwards)

1. Objective

To provide financial assistance to meritorious students from poor families to meet a

part of their day-to-day expenses while pursuing higher studies.

2. Scope

The scholarships are awarded by Ministry of Education, Government of India on the

basis of results of Higher Secondary / Class XII Board Examination. A maximum of

82,000 fresh scholarships per annum are provided for pursuing graduate /

postgraduate degree in colleges and universities and for professional courses, such as

Medical, Engineering etc.

3. Allocation of Scholarship

The total number of scholarships are divided amongst the State Education Boards

based on the State’s population in the age group of 18-25 years, after segregating

share of CBSE and ICSE on the basis of number of students passing out from various

Boards in the country. 50% of the scholarships are earmarked for girls. Out of the

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
total scholarship slots earmarked for UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, 3% slots

shall be earmarked for the students from the UT of Ladakh. The number of

scholarships allotted to a State Education Board is distributed amongst pass outs of

the Humanities, Science and Commerce streams in the ratio of 3:3:1. In case of

shortfall in the number of applications, the scholarship slots shall be interoperable

among categories (Gen, OBC, SC & ST), gender (Female, Male) and State Quota to

maximize use of slots for fresh scholarships with effect from academic year 2022-23,

subject to the condition that guidelines of Ministry of Finance and NITI Aayog

regarding SC/ST fund allocation of the schemes are adhered to.

4. Eligibility for Scholarship
i. Students who are above 80th percentile of successful candidates in the relevant

stream from the respective Board of Examination in Class XII of 10+2 pattern or

equivalent;

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
ii. Pursuing regular degree courses and not correspondence or distance mode or

pursuing Diploma courses;

iii. Pursuing courses at colleges/institutions recognized by All India Council for

Technical Education and respective Regulatory Bodies concerned;

iv. Not availing benefit of any other scholarship schemes including State run

scholarship schemes/ fee waiver & reimbursement scheme;

v. Students with gross parental/family income upto Rs. 4.5 lakh per annum are

eligible for scholarship under the scheme. Income certificate will be required only

for the fresh applicants;

vi. Student changing his/ her college/institute of study will be allowed to

continue/renew the scholarship provided the course of study and the institution is

having valid AISHE Code; The AISHE code can be checked in the portal

https://aishe.gov.in/aishe/aisheCode

vii. Students who missed to apply for renewal of application online on NSP will be

allowed to apply for renewal of scholarship for subsequent year on NSP, if he/she

fulfils eligibility condition for renewal;

viii. For renewal of scholarship in each year of study, besides getting at least 50%

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
marks in the Annual Examination, maintenance of adequate attendance of at least

75%, will also be the criteria. Complaints against the student regarding any in

disciplined or criminal behaviour including any complaints of having indulged in

ragging, will lead to forfeiture of scholarship;

ix. Beneficiaries/ Applicants under the scheme must apply online in the National

Scholarships Portal (www.scholarships.gov.in) for the fresh/ renewal scholarships.

Fresh/Renewal applications sent directly to the Ministry of Education shall not be

accepted.

5. Reservation

Students belonging to reserved categories/weaker sections /minorities etc. are eligible

to get benefit of reservation on the basis of merit, subject to Central Reservation

Policy [i.e. 15% seats are earmarked for SCs, 7.5% for STs and 27 % for OBCs and

5% horizontal reservation for Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) in all the categories].

The Central Reservation Policy will be applicable in filling the slots against each

year's target. If slots under a specific group is not filled after considering all the

States/UTs, the vacant slots will be allocated to other categories so that maximum

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text: number of eligible students can get the benefit, subject to overall ceiling of slots.

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
6. Procedure for Application

i. The applications are received online only. Verification of credentials of the

students like caste, educational qualifications etc. are done through

DIGILOCKER facility of the MeITY, Govt. of India.

ii. National Scholarships Portal (NSP) (www.scholarships.gov.in) will provide the

timelines for opening & closing of the portal.

iii. The Guidelines for application, verification, selection and disbursement of

scholarship will be as per the NSP.

iv. Selection list would be generated/displayed on NSP.

v. Online applications will be verified at two levels i.e by the Institute, where the

student is studying and thereafter by the concerned State Higher Education

Department or any other Agency/ Official nominated by the State as State Nodal

Agency (both for fresh and renewal applicants).

vi. Latest guideline on Timelines will be made available on NSP.

vii. Students will not be permanently debarred for scholarships due to delay to renew

or verification. However, students will have to submit renewal applications within

a cut-off date. Renewal for that year will not be allowed if an applicant misses this

deadline.

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
7. Rate and Duration of Scholarship (from financial year 2022-23)

The rate of scholarship is Rs.12,000/-per annum at Graduation level for first three

years of College and University courses and Rs.20,000/-per annum at Post-

Graduation level. Students pursuing professional courses, in case, where the duration

of course is five (5) years/Integrated course will get Rs. 20,000/-per annum in the
4th and 5th year. However, students pursuing technical courses such as B.Tech,
B.Engg. will get scholarship up to graduation level only i.e. Rs. 12,000 p.a. for 1st,
2nd and 3rd year and Rs. 20,000 in the 4th year.

Note: The rate of scholarship is Rs.10,000/-per annum for first three years of fresh/

renewal scholarships with respect to academic year 2021-22, even if the actual release

happens in FY 2022-23.

8. Payment of Scholarship

Students are required to have the bank accounts opened, especially, in their name for

availing the benefits under the scheme. The scholarship will be disbursed directly into

the savings bank accounts of the beneficiaries through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)

ministry_department: Ministry of Education
text:
mode. The student can track their payment status from the template “Know Your

Payment” in the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) portal

[ https://pfms.nic.in/Users/LoginDetails/Login.aspx] either by indicating Aadhaar

number or bank account number or NSP Application ID.

9. For Colleges/Universities

College and Universities will apprise the students about the “PM-USP CSSS” during

admission. Aadhaar based authentication of Institute Nodal Officer (INO)/ State

Nodal Officer (SNO) is mandatory for every Institution/State before verification of

the applications. INO/SNO should be a regular employee.

10. For State Government/State Boards

Adequate publicity of the scheme may be initiated through the Schools/ Colleges/

Institutions to create awareness and to facilitate/ assist the applicants in rural area to

apply for scholarship online on NSP.

11. Grievance Redressal

In case of any grievances/complaint regarding the above scheme, the same may be

registered to the following link:

http://pgportal.gov.in/grievancenew.aspx

other than to the Nodal Officer whose email is available on NSP portal

(Services Tab).

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
In exercise of the powers conferred under Section 21 and Section 35A of the Banking
Regulation Act, 1949, and of all the powers enabling it in this behalf, the Reserve Bank
of India, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest and in
the interest of banking policy to do so, hereby, issues the Directions hereinafter
specified.

Chapter I: Preliminary

A. Short Title and Commencement

1. These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India [Commercial Banks -
Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme] Directions, 2026.

2. The Directions shall be applicable to loans sanctioned under the KCC Scheme with
effect from January 01, 2027. Loans sanctioned prior to the said date shall continue
to be governed by the extant guidelines till maturity / next renewal.

B. Objective

3. These Directions are issued with a view to laying down the framework for adequate
and timely credit support from the banking system to be provided under the KCC
Scheme to meet the working capital and investment credit needs of borrowers
engaged in agriculture and allied activities, through a composite facility, requiring
simple and standard procedure.

C. Applicability

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
4. These Directions shall be applicable to all Commercial Banks (hereinafter
collectively referred to as ‘banks’ and individually as a ‘bank’)

For the purpose of these Directions, ‘Commercial Banks’ mean banking companies
(other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks)
corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India, as defined respectively under
clauses (c), (da) and (nc) of Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act,1949.

5. These Directions shall not be applicable to operations of overseas branches of
Indian banks.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
D. Definitions/Clarifications

6. For the purpose of these Directions, unless the context or subject otherwise
requires, the terms herein shall bear the meanings assigned to them as given below:

(1) “Crop season” means the period up to harvesting and marketing of the crops
raised.

(2) “Short duration crops” shall mean crops with anticipated duration from sowing to
marketing up to twelve months.

(3) “Long duration” crops mean crops which are not short duration crops. The crop
season for long duration crops i.e., anticipated period from sowing to marketing is
more than twelve months and up to eighteen months.

(4) For the purpose of the KCC Scheme, crop seasons shall be standardized at twelve
months for short duration crops and eighteen months for long duration crops.

(5) “Marginal farmer” means a farmer with landholding of up to one hectare.

(6) “Small farmer” means a farmer with landholding of more than one hectare and up
to two hectares.

7. Words and expressions used herein and not defined in these Directions, but defined
in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, or the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, shall
have the meanings assigned to them in those Acts.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
Chapter II: Credit - Purpose, Tenure and Limit

E. Purpose and Tenure

8. Under the KCC Scheme, banks shall extend credit to eligible borrowers for their
farming and other needs as indicated below in the form of a composite facility with a
tenure of six years:

(1) Short term credit requirements for cultivation of crops;

(2) Short term credit requirements for allied activities, an indicative list of which is
provided in the table below:

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
S.No Allied activity Purpose
(i) Animal Husbandry Rearing of dairy animals / poultry birds / small
ruminants; illustratively, cattle, buffalo, camel, yak,
mithun, goat, sheep, pig, rabbit, etc.
(ii) Fisheries & Rearing and capturing of fish / shrimp / other aquatic
Aquaculture organisms; illustratively, fish culture, composite /
integrated fish culture, polyculture, raceways fish
culture, sea cage culture, cage / pen culture in
reservoir, wetland fisheries, ornamental fish farming,
fish angling, fish seed rearing, saline water aquaculture
(shrimp / fish), shrimp culture, prawn culture, pearl
culture, crab culture, seaweed cultivation, aquaponics,
bio-floc fish farming, bivalve culture and brackish water
culture, etc., and other production related activities
concerned with inland / marine fisheries and
aquaculture.
(iii) Other allied activities Production related activities concerned with sericulture,
lac culture, beekeeping, and similar other allied
activities.

(3) Post-harvest / post- production expenses;

(4) Consumption requirements of farmer household;

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(5) Expenses for maintenance of assets related to agriculture and allied activities, soil
testing, real time weather forecasts / other technological support services and organic
/ good agricultural practices or similar relevant certification;

(6) Crop insurance, accident insurance, health insurance and asset insurance;

(7) Produce marketing loans; and

(8) Investment requirements for agriculture and allied activities.

9. The aggregate of components at (1) to (7) above shall form the short-term credit
limit portion of the composite facility and the component at (8) shall constitute the long-
term credit limit portion of the facility.

10. The short-term credit limit fixed for the sixth year together with the estimated long-
term credit limit shall be the Composite Maximum Permissible Limit (CMPL) and is to
be treated as the KCC limit.
Note: Refer D of illustrations 1 and 2 given in the Annex I.

11. The short-term component of the KCC limit for the purposes of crop cultivation and
allied activities shall be in the nature of revolving cash credit facility. There shall be no
restriction on the number of debits and credits.

F. Working capital for cultivation of crops

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
12. Eligibility

The following shall be eligible to avail credit for working capital requirements for
cultivation of crops:
(1) Farmers (individual / joint borrowers), who are owner cultivators;

(2) Tenant farmers, oral lessees, and sharecroppers; and

(3) Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) of farmers / cultivators
including tenant farmers, oral lessees, and sharecroppers.

13. Fixation of Drawing Limit

(1) The drawing limit for each crop season shall be the sum total of the following:

(i) Scale of Finance (SoF) [as notified by State Level Technical Committee
(SLTC) / District Level Technical Committee (DLTC)] for the respective
crop/s for the current crop season multiplied by extent of area of cultivation
5

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(ii) 10 per cent of (i) above towards post-harvest expenses and consumption
requirements of household
(iii) 20 per cent of (i) above towards repairs and maintenance of farm assets,
soil testing, weather advisory and agri-extension service subscriptions,
software and digital advisory platforms fees, drone-based crop health
surveys and spraying services, remote sensing and satellite-based crop
monitoring services, other technological support services, organic / good
agricultural practices certification and similar other services, in the nature of
working capital expenses.
(iv) Premium for crop insurance, accident insurance, health insurance and asset
insurance, if any.

(2) In case the cropping pattern adopted by the farmer changes for any subsequent
season, the drawing limit shall be reworked by taking into consideration the crops
proposed to be grown.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(3) In situations where the SoF has not been notified by SLTC for a particular crop
season, at the time of the farmer availing the loan, the bank shall consider applying a
10 per cent notional hike over the SoF applicable for the previous season and
determine the drawable limit for the ensuing season. However, in cases where the
SoF has been notified but not revised, banks shall adopt the existing SoF.

(4) In respect of crops not covered in the SoF finalised by the SLTC / DLTC of the
respective State, loans extended shall be outside the KCC framework. However,
efforts must be made to get the SoF of such crops notified by the SLTC / DLTC.

(5) The KCC credit limit shall be rounded off to the nearest ₹1,000.

(6) At the time of sanction, the maximum permissible limit (MPL) for the short-term
crop loan shall be arrived at on a notional basis by adding 10 per cent to the limit of
the previous crop season, from the second crop season onwards. In case the drawing
limit exceeds the MPL in any crop season / year, the MPL shall be reassessed at the
time of review.

Note: Refer A (I), (II), (III) and (IV) of Illustrations 1 and 2 given in the Annex I.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(7) Marginal farmers shall also be eligible for a flexible credit limit of ₹10,000 to
₹50,000 (as Flexi KCC) as per assessment of the bank without relating it to the value
of the land. The credit limit shall be based on crops grown, post-harvest warehouse

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
storage related credit needs, other farm expenses, consumption needs and
investment requirements for agriculture and allied activities. The composite KCC limit
is to be fixed for a period of six years on this basis. Wherever higher limit is required
due to change in cropping pattern and / or SoF, the limit may be arrived at as per the
estimation indicated at paragraphs 13(1) to 13(6).

14. Repayment Period

Banks shall fix the repayment period as per the crop season applicable.

G. Working Capital for Allied Activities

15. Eligibility

The following borrowers shall be eligible to avail credit for working capital requirements
for allied activities.

(1) Animal husbandry farmers, fishers, fish farmers and farmers (including tenant
farmers and sharecroppers), undertaking allied activities as per para 8(2) as individual
/ joint borrowers; and

(2) SHGs / JLGs of individuals as above.

16. Fixation of Drawing Limit

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(1) Banks shall fix the drawing limits for allied activities based on the SoF (as notified
by SLTC / DLTC) for the respective activities and number of units (acre / unit / animal
/ bird, etc.) by adopting the method analogous to that of working capital loans for
cultivation of crops as indicated at paragraph 13 above.

(2) In respect of allied activities not covered in the SoF finalised by the SLTC / DLTC
of the respective State, loans extended shall be outside the KCC framework. However,
efforts must be made to get the SoF of such allied activities notified by the SLTC /
DLTC.

(3) In cases where a borrower avails credit for both crop cultivation and allied activities
under the KCC framework, the additional component towards consumption
requirements (10 per cent) shall be considered only once and shall not be reckoned
separately for each activity.

Note: Refer B (I), (II), (III) and (IV) of Illustrations 1 and 2 given in the Annex I.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(4) The drawing power for the working capital limit for allied activities shall be
determined based on the SoF / latest valuation of stocks / receivables / cash flows as
per terms of sanction.

17. Repayment Period

Banks shall fix the repayment period as per the cash flow / income generation pattern
of the activity undertaken by the borrower.

H. Investment Credit for Agriculture and Allied Activities

18. Eligibility

Beneficiaries specified in paragraph 12 and 15 above shall be eligible to avail
investment credit for purposes related to agriculture and allied activities, illustratively:

(1) land development
(2) minor irrigation
(3) purchase of farm / fishing, etc., equipment
(4) construction of animal / bird shed
(5) purchase of livestock
(6) purchase of equipment related to allied activities, and
(7) similar other purposes

19. Fixation of Limit

(1) The term loan limit shall be based on the proposed investment(s) during the tenure
of the KCC facility and the bank's assessment of the repaying capacity of the borrower.

Note: Refer C (I), (II) and (III) of Illustrations 1 and 2 given in the Annex I.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
(2) The draw down of instalments shall be allowed based on the nature of investment.

20. Repayment Period

The term-loan component shall be repayable within a period of six years depending
on the type of activity / investment, as per the bank’s credit policy applicable for
investment credit. If the nature of investment involves a tenure longer than six years,
the term loan may be treated as a separate facility outside the KCC framework.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
Chapter III: General Instructions

I. Rate of Interest

21. The rate of interest shall be as stipulated in Reserve Bank of India (Commercial
Banks - Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, as
amended from time to time and as per other relevant guidelines issued in respect of
charging interest on agricultural advances.

22. Banks shall pay interest on the minimum credit balance in KCC cash credit
accounts as stipulated in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest
Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 17, 2026), as amended from
time to time.

J. Collateral Security and Margin

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
23. Banks shall waive collateral security and margin requirements for agricultural loans
including loans for allied activities up to ₹2 lakh per borrower. However, voluntary
pledge of gold and silver as collateral for agriculture loans up to the collateral-free limit
will not be considered as a violation of the guidelines on collateral-free lending to the
agriculture sector. Banks shall obtain and retain explicit declaration from the borrower
in such cases. RBI guidelines on collateral free limit pertain only to secondary
collateral and not primary security or assets financed by the loan.

24. Banks shall decide the collateral security and margin requirements for loans above
₹2 lakh as per their credit policy and in adherence with RBI guidelines issued from
time to time.

25. In case of KCC loans against hypothecation of crops / stock and involving tie-up
arrangements for recovery, banks may waive collateral security for loans up to a limit
of ₹3 lakh.

K. Segregation of Limits

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
26. Considering the different interest rates and repayment schedules applicable to
various types of credit provided under KCC, the facility may be divided into sub-limits
for short-term cash credit limit-cum-savings accounts for crop cultivation and allied
activities separately, and long-term loan for agriculture and allied activities. For

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
operational convenience, these sub-limits shall be maintained as separate loan
accounts under the composite KCC facility.

L. Monitoring of End Utilization

27. Banks shall ensure ongoing monitoring of the end use of the credit facility by the
borrower as per the terms of sanction through field inspections and / or other means,
as per their credit policy.

M. Review and Renewal

28. Banks shall undertake review and renewal of the short-term limits for crop
cultivation and allied activities as per their credit policy.

N. Other instructions

29. Banks shall obtain a one-time documentation including land record / tenancy
certificate / equivalent certificate as per their credit policy at the time of application for
fresh loan. During the tenure of the facility, at the time of each review, the bank shall
obtain declaration from the borrower(s) regarding proposed activity / activities.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
30. In case of loans to sharecroppers and oral lessees, banks shall accept certificates
provided by local administration / panchayati raj institutions regarding the cultivation
of crops by such borrowers. Where there are difficulties in getting certification
regarding identity and occupational status of sharecroppers and oral lessees, banks
shall accept an affidavit submitted by such borrowers giving their occupational status
(i.e., details of land tilled / crops grown), for loans up to ₹50,000.

31. Processing fees, inspection charges and other charges shall be as per the bank’s
policy on applicable charges and applicable regulatory guidelines, if any.

32. The KCC holder will have the option to avail any type of crop insurance, asset
insurance, accident insurance (including Personal Accident Insurance Scheme) or
health insurance and may pay the premium through the KCC account. Beneficiaries
shall be made aware of the insurance covers available. Their explicit consent shall be
obtained, at the application stage itself if the premium is to be paid through the KCC
account.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
33. In case insurance (crop insurance, asset insurance and personal accident
insurance) is funded under the KCC facility, the same shall be assigned in favour of
the lending bank.

34. Draw down of the limit shall be allowed as per the convenience of the farmer using
any of the following delivery channels:

(1) operation through banking outlet / part-time banking outlet (as defined in the
Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
dated November 28, 2025, as amended from time to time). and business
correspondents

(2) operation through ATMs / micro-ATMs / PoS terminals, etc. in an interoperable
manner

(3) mobile based transactions at agricultural input dealers and mandis

(4) operation through any other permitted digital delivery channel

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
35. Banks shall enable operations in KCC accounts through Unified Payments
Interface (for working capital credit), debit cards (as stipulated in Reserve Bank of India
(Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct)
Directions, 2025 dated November 28,2025, as amended from time to time), mobile
banking, internet banking, National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT), Real Time
Gross Settlement (RTGS), Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) or any other
regulated digital delivery channel, after obtaining explicit consent of the account
holder.

36. In case the farmer applies for loan against the warehouse receipt of the produce,
the bank shall consider such request as per established procedure and guidelines.
The loan extended to the farmer in such case shall be linked with the related short-
term KCC loan, if any, and the outstanding amount in such loan shall be adjusted at
the time of disbursal of the loan secured by warehouse receipt.

37. Banks shall adhere to the instructions regarding interest subvention and prompt
repayment incentive on KCC loans, as applicable from time to time.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
38. Prudential norms on income recognition, asset-classification and provisioning as
stipulated in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Asset Classification,
Provisioning and Income Recognition) Directions, 2026 dated April 27, 2026, as
amended from time to time, shall apply to loans granted under the KCC Scheme.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
Chapter IV: Disclosure, Exemptions, Repeal and other Provisions

O. Data Reporting

39. Banks shall submit data on KCC loans as per the prescribed reporting format, at
quarterly intervals, within 15 working days from the end of the quarter.

P. Exemptions
40. The Reserve Bank may, if it considers necessary for avoiding any hardship or for
any other just and sufficient reason, grant extension of time to comply with or exempt
any regulated entity, from all or any of the provisions of these Directions either
generally or for any specified period, subject to such conditions as the Reserve Bank
may impose.

Q. Repeal

41. The list of circulars repealed with respect to the provisions relating to commercial
banks coming under the purview of this Direction is given in Appendix.

42. The Directions, instructions, and guidelines repealed prior to the issuance of these
Directions shall continue to remain repealed.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
43. Notwithstanding such repeal, any action taken or purported to have been taken,
or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to
be governed by the provisions thereof. All approvals or acknowledgements granted
under these repealed lists shall be deemed as governed by these Directions. Further,
the repeal of these Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall not in any way
prejudicially affect:

(1) any right, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, or incurred thereunder.,

(2) any, penalty, forfeiture, or punishment incurred in respect of any contravention
committed thereunder; and

(3) any investigation, legal proceeding, or remedy in respect of any such right,
privilege, obligation, liability, penalty, forfeiture, or punishment as aforesaid; and any
such investigation, legal proceedings or remedy may be instituted, continued, or
enforced and any such penalty, forfeiture, or punishment may be imposed as if those
Directions, instructions, or guidelines had not been repealed.

ministry_department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
text:
R. Application of other laws not barred

44. The provisions of these Directions shall be in addition to, and not in derogation
of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations or Directions, for the time being
in force.

S. Interpretations

45. For the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of these Directions or in order
to remove any difficulties in the application or interpretation of the provisions of these
Directions, the Reserve Bank may, if it considers necessary, issue necessary
clarifications in respect of any matter covered herein and the interpretation of any
provision of these Directions given by the Reserve Bank shall be final and binding.

(Nisha Nambiar)
Chief General Manager-in-Charge

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP), launched in August 1995, was designed to provide

a safety net for the most disadvantaged and vulnerable sections of Indian society. Currently, NSAP has

five major schemes under its ambit: Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS), Indira

Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS), Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme

(IGNDPS), National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS), and the Annapurna Scheme. Over the years, NSAP

has evolved into a key pillar of India’s social protection architecture, with substantial financial outlays

aimed at ensuring basic income security for the poorest households. However, the Comptroller and

Auditor General (CAG) of India’s 2023 performance audit revealed wide state-level disparities and

several systemic gaps in planning, financial management, and monitoring. The audit found instances

of both exclusions where eligible beneficiaries were left out and inclusion errors where ineligible

persons received benefits due to weaknesses in verification, data maintenance, and authentication

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
systems. Additionally, irregularities in payment schedules and partial non-compliance with Direct

Benefit Transfer (DBT) mechanisms were noted, prompting a series of corrective recommendations

from the CAG. Against this backdrop, a regular independent evaluation of NSAP was critical to gauge

its effectiveness, assess progress toward its objectives, and identify measures to enhance delivery and

accountability. In this context, the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) commissioned Academy of

Management Studies (AMS) to undertake an Impact Assessment and Evaluation of NSAP to assess the

programme’s achievements and recommend actionable strategies for its strengthening and

continuation.

The broad objectives of the study were to:

➢ Analyze the achievements of NSAP objectives,

➢ Assess scheme-level implementation, and

➢ Recommend measures to enhance scheme delivery and accountability.

The study employed a mixed-methods approach across ten sample states representing different

pension categories, such as Haryana, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh (high), Gujarat, Jammu &

Kashmir, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh (moderate), and Assam, Chhattisgarh and Bihar (low). Data

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
collection combined structured surveys with 6,000 beneficiaries across 600 Gram Panchayats (GPs),

semi-structured interviews with local elected representatives, focus group discussions with

community members, and in-depth interviews with district and state level officials to capture both

implementation realities and administrative perspectives.

i

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
Key findings of the study, mapped against the broad objectives, have been depicted below –

I. Analysis of the achievements of the objectives of NSAP

Reducing financial dependency - About 75.1% of beneficiaries reported that the pension has

somewhat reduced their dependence on other earning members of the household, while 16.5% said

it has significantly lowered their financial dependency. These findings highlight that even modest

financial support under NSAP enhances beneficiaries’ financial autonomy and household stability. In

states such as Andhra Pradesh and Haryana, where higher state top-ups ranging from ₹1,000 to ₹3,000

per month are provided, the scheme has led to notable improvements in beneficiary satisfaction.

Improvement in Socio-economic status- NSAP pensions have contributed to increased household

consumption, improved healthcare access, and enhanced food adequacy, as the study finds that 81-

84% of beneficiaries spent the pension amount for food and medicine. A majority of beneficiaries

reported better access to food (63%), an increased capacity to purchase daily commodities (68%),

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
and improved access to medical care (65%). The scheme has also reduced the need to borrow for

subsistence among half of the respondents. States such as Jammu & Kashmir, Telangana, and Tamil

Nadu recorded particularly strong outcomes, with over 70-90% of beneficiaries reporting

improvement in these areas.

Ensuring Dignity, Social Security and Safety- Across states, around 67-69% of beneficiaries reported

an improvement in their social acceptance, treatment within the family, and self-esteem, reflecting

how the pension contributes to restoring self-worth and social security. States such as Jammu &

Kashmir, and Telangana showed widespread positive changes, indicating strong social recognition and

empowerment among beneficiaries. However, 13.3% of beneficiaries reported being able to save any

portion of their pension, indicating that while the scheme supports basic sustenance, the amount

remains largely inadequate.

II. Scheme level Analysis

Beneficiary Awareness - Awareness level about NSAP schemes is moderate but uneven across states.

31.6% of beneficiaries were aware of the scheme implementing department, and only about half

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
knew about the central and state contribution components. Awareness levels were high in Andhra

Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu, where active community engagement and outreach through

local institutions and digital campaigns have helped strengthen information flow. In contrast, limited

awareness was observed in states like Bihar, Chhattisgarh, and Gujarat.

Implementation framework and eligibility- The NSAP framework is found to be effectively

implemented across most states, with clear administrative responsibilities at state, district, and Gram

Panchayat levels. However, the study observed inconsistencies in beneficiary identification due to

reliance on outdated Below Poverty Line (BPL) lists. Almost all the states covered in this study follows

ii

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
the BPL criteria. Though a very few instances of exclusion of eligible and inclusion of ineligible

beneficiaries were reported, states such as Haryana, which use a Family ID database for automatic

verification, have shown higher accuracy and transparency in targeting.

Disbursement, DBT and Beneficiary Convenience - The implementation of Direct Benefit Transfer

(DBT) across all states (except Andhra Pradesh) has improved transparency and accountability in

pension delivery, with 97% of beneficiaries reporting that their Aadhaar is linked to their bank or

post office accounts. However, delays in pension disbursement were observed in some states due to

connectivity issues, biometric authentication failures, and administrative bottlenecks. Andhra

Pradesh and Haryana stood out for ensuring timely and predictable payments, including doorstep

delivery of pensions for the elderly and persons with disabilities. In contrast, states such as Jammu &

Kashmir and Assam continue to face challenges related to accessibility of financial institutions. Long-

distance travel to collect pensions remains a major challenge in Gujarat, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu,

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
affecting over 60% of beneficiaries and adding to their financial and physical hardship.

Satisfaction and Adequacy - 73% of the beneficiaries surveyed were satisfied with the overall

process of the pension scheme. However, the majority also reported that the pension amount is

insufficient to meet essential needs such as food, healthcare, and utilities. 89% of the beneficiaries

believed that the government should contribute more funds to increase the pension amount and

improve related services. Beneficiaries in states with higher state top-ups (Andhra Pradesh,

Telangana, Tamil Nadu) showed significantly greater satisfaction and improved well-being compared

to those in low-top-up states (Assam, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh).

Social Audit- The study also found that social audits are not conducted regularly across many states,

limiting community oversight and accountability. Overall, 53.5% of gram panchayat and ward officials

confirmed that a social audit had been conducted, while 30.7% reported none, and 15.8% were

unaware. The highest incidence of social audits was recorded in Assam (86.7%), Uttar Pradesh (80%),

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
and Andhra Pradesh (76.7%), indicating a relatively strong monitoring and transparency in these

states.

Grievance Redressal- 377 out of 600 panchayat and ward officials reported having a grievance

redressal system in place. Mechanisms were most prevalent in Assam (95%), Andhra Pradesh (90%),

and Telangana (90%), while Jammu & Kashmir (0%) and Tamil Nadu (46.7%) lagged significantly.

Gram Sabha meetings emerged as the most common platform for raising grievances (reported by

80.1% of officials), with delays in pension disbursement being the most common concern among

beneficiaries.

Best Practices- In Jammu & Kashmir, awareness about the scheme is widely promoted through print,

electronic, and community-based platforms such as Anganwadi and ASHA workers. Haryana has

introduced a transparent Family ID system that automatically updates beneficiary information with

minimum interference form gram panchayat and ward officials, ensuring fair and efficient delivery.

iii

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
In Andhra Pradesh and Haryana, pension disbursement mechanisms are highly efficient, with doorstep

delivery of benefits for elderly and disabled persons who cannot travel.

III. Recommendations & Way Forward

Justification for the continuation of the scheme: Despite India’s rapid economic growth, the central

pension component has remained unchanged since 2012, leading to significant decline in its real value

due to inflation and rising living costs. Strengthening and expanding NSAP is therefore critical to ensuring

dignity and social security for vulnerable citizens. Moreover, aligning pension levels with inflation, poverty

benchmarks, and international norms will make the scheme more adequate and equitable.

Recommendations on improving the scheme implementation: The Below Poverty Line (BPL) criteria

should be replaced with a more reliable and integrated beneficiary identification system based on

verified databases such as Aadhaar, social registries, or state Family ID systems to ensure accurate

targeting and reduce duplication. The criteria and verification process may be left to the discretion

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
of individual states. To ensure last-mile efficiency, beneficiary facilitation centres at village or ward

levels could be established to assist the elderly, widows, and persons with disabilities in registration,

documentation, and grievance redressal. The pension amount should be suitably revised by

introducing a National Floor Pension, linked to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and periodically

adjusted to reflect the cost of living, thereby ensuring a decent standard of life. Mechanisms for

doorstep pension delivery, as practiced in Haryana and Andhra Pradesh, should be adopted by other

states to support beneficiaries with mobility challenges. Further, convergence with other welfare

schemes such as PMAY, NFSA, health insurance, and other livelihood programmes should be

established to enhance social and economic resilience. The grievance redressal system should be

made more accessible through toll-free helplines, Panchayat-level complaint cells, and escalation

protocols integrated with the NSAP-PPS portal. Regular social audits, data-driven monitoring

dashboards, and periodic third-party evaluations should be institutionalized to ensure transparency,

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
accountability, and continuous improvement in scheme delivery.

In conclusion, the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) continues to play a significant role in

India’s social protection framework, contributing to poverty reduction and providing social security to

the elderly, widows, and persons with disabilities. However, the study highlights the need to

strengthen key areas such as beneficiary identification, timely disbursement of pensions, and proper

maintenance of records to improve efficiency and transparency. Enhancing convergence with state

schemes, ensuring regular indexation of pension amounts to inflation, and adopting a robust

monitoring and grievance redressal system will be crucial to achieving the scheme’s goal of ensuring

a life of dignity and security for all vulnerable citizens.

* * * * *

1 CHAPTER

Context – Background Study

1.1 INTRODUCTION

The National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) derives its mandate from Article 41 of the
Constitution, as part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)1, which states that “the State

shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing

the right to…public assistance in case of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in

other cases of undeserved want.” Although not enforceable in the court of law as a Fundamental
Right, Prabhat Patnaik (2018)2 argues that “adequate pension to the elderly is an economic right”,

which is “not codified as such in the Constitution”, but “implicit and as fundamental as the explicitly-

codified fundamental rights”. To fulfil the constitutional obligation, Government of India introduced

NSAP in 1995 as a welfare programme aimed at providing basic financial support to the destitutes and

BPL households. The scheme is being implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD). It

includes 3 pension schemes targeting old aged (above 60 years), widows, and disabled persons living

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
below poverty line. In addition, a family benefit scheme offering one-time assistance to the bereaved

family in the event of death of the breadwinner is also included under the ambit of NSAP.

As per the CAG report of 2023, during 2017-21, Government of India allocated ₹ 34,432 crore for

NSAP. In addition to this ₹ 1,09,573 crore was allocated by States and UTs to offer additional

assistance for pension and for covering beneficiaries that were left out from the coverage of

NSAP. A total of 2.83 crore beneficiaries were covered annually through funds allocated by central

government, and additional 1.82 crore beneficiaries were covered through States/UTs funds. The

coverage of the scheme spans across both, urban and rural areas across all states and UTs in the

country. The beneficiaries for the scheme are identified on the basis of BPL list prepared by the

states and UTs as per guidelines issued by the MoRD for rural areas and by the Ministry of Urban

Housing & Poverty Alleviation for urban areas. In addition, the states also have the power to

identify additional eligible beneficiaries in case they identify cases where the person’s name is not

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
included in the BPL list, but he or she satisfies the given eligibility criteria.

1 The DPSP are a set of guidelines in Part IV of the Indian Constitution (Art. 36 – 51) that aim to create a welfare state by
promoting socio-economic justice.
2 Patnaik, P. (2018). The great pension scandal: A laughable pittance of Rs. 200 a month!. News click. Accessed at
https://www.newsclick.in/great-pension-scandal-laughable-pittance-rs-200-month

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
The Ministry releases scheme-wise funds to all states/UTs as per the estimated number of

beneficiaries under each scheme on an annual basis. According to NSAP guidelines, the States/UTs

are encouraged to provide an additional amount at least equivalent to the assistance provided by the

Central Government so that the beneficiaries can get a decent level of assistance. The Programme

aims to achieve universal coverage of eligible persons through proactive identification. The

Programme also seeks to have automatic convergence with other schemes to provide

maximum benefit to the beneficiaries.

1.1.1 Components of NSAP

The National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) comprises five major sub-schemes aimed at providing

financial and food security support to vulnerable sections of the population. These include:

➢ Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): Offers financial assistance of ₹200

per month to individuals aged 60–79 years and ₹500 per month to those aged 80 and above.

Currently, more than 221 lakh beneficiaries are covered.

➢ Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS): Provides ₹300 per month to widows

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
aged 40–79 years and ₹500 to those 80 and above. Currently, more than 67 lakh

beneficiaries are covered.

➢ Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS): Financial assistance of ₹300 per month

to individuals with severe or multiple disabilities aged 18–79 and ₹500 to those aged 80

years and above. Currently, more than 8.8 lakh beneficiaries are covered.

➢ National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS): Grants one-time financial assistance of ₹20,000 to

bereaved families upon the death of the primary breadwinner aged between 18 and 59

years. The upper limit of households is 3.58 lakh.

➢ Annapurna Scheme: Provided 10 kg of food grains per month free of cost to those senior

citizens who, though eligible, were not receiving old age pension. It was a demand-based

scheme with an upper limit of 8.32 lakh beneficiaries.

However, there has been no uptake of the scheme since 2019. This may be attributed to the fact

that most households now receive food grains under the National Food Security Act (NFSA),

which, while not part of NSAP, effectively addresses their food security needs.

Initially launched as a centrally sponsored scheme, NSAP underwent several changes, including

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
the transfer of the National Maternity Benefit Scheme to the Department of Family Welfare, the

introduction of Annapurna in 2000, and its devolution to state plans in 2002–03. In 2007, coverage

was expanded to all BPL persons, and in 2009, pensions for widows and persons with disabilities

were introduced. The scheme specifically targets Below Poverty Line (BPL) individuals and
continues to evolve to address the needs of India’s most vulnerable populations.3

3 https://nsap.gov.in

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
1.1.2 Funding & Coverage

The National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) has undergone significant changes in its funding

and coverage since its inception. Initially transferred to the State Plan in 2002, funds were routed

through the Ministry of Finance for States and the Ministry of Home Affairs for Union Territories until

2013–14. However, from 1st April 2014, NSAP was converted into a Centrally Sponsored Scheme

(CSS), and since then, the Ministry of Rural Development has been directly releasing funds to States

and UTs. Notably, in December 2016, NSAP was designated as a “Core of the Core” scheme by NITI

Aayog. Currently, the allocation of central assistance is based on either the State Cap or the digitized

number of beneficiaries on the NSAP-Pension Payment System (PPS), whichever is lower. The State

Cap, i.e., the number of beneficiaries under each scheme for each State/UT is derived using the 2001

Census population and the poverty ratio as estimated by the erstwhile Planning Commission.

Currently, NSAP provides pensions to approximately 3 crores Below Poverty Line (BPL) beneficiaries,

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
and States determine the estimated number of beneficiaries for the following year based on reports

from the previous year. In addition to the central support, States supplement the pension amount,

ranging from ₹50 to ₹5700 per month, and extend coverage to additional beneficiaries using their

own resources. This has enabled around 5.87 crore additional pensioners to be covered under

various State-run schemes, bringing the total number of beneficiaries receiving pension support

under NSAP and State schemes to nearly 9 crores. The three pension schemes namely, IGNOAPS,

IGNDPS and IGNWPS are 100% saturated. However, National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS) is

demand based. To improve transparency and ensure faster transactions, the NSAP pension
schemes were brought under the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) schemes in December 2014. 4Many

state governments have their own social pension schemes for vulnerable groups. Hence, there

remains significant variation across States in eligibility criteria, assistance norms, and benefit

amounts, reflecting diverse policy approaches to social assistance.

Budget Allocation

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
The budget allocation for the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) has remained largely

stagnant between FY 2021-22 and FY 2024-25, reflecting limited fiscal expansion in social pensions.

Under IGNOAPS, allocations stabilized around ₹6,600–₹7,000 crore in subsequent years, constituting

nearly 70% of the total NSAP budget.

Similar stability is observed under IGNWPS and IGNDPS, with allocations around ₹2,000 crore and

₹290 crore, respectively, indicating no major enhancement in benefit size or coverage. In contrast, the

National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS) shows fluctuating allocations, with a notable reduction in

2024-25 (RE) to ₹300 crore, suggesting lower uptake or delayed disbursal, while the Annapurna

Scheme has become almost nominal at ₹10 crore, signaling its near phase-out.

4 NSAP Social Audit Guidelines 2023, https://nsap.nic.in/

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development

Overall, total NSAP allocation has remained around ₹9,000-₹9,650 crore over the last four years, with

minimal variation between Budget and Revised Estimates. When adjusted for inflation, this stagnation

translates into a real-term decline in social protection spending. The trend underscores that while the

programme continues to provide a safety net for elderly, widows, and persons with disabilities, its

fiscal prioritization has weakened over time, highlighting the need for enhanced budgetary support,

periodic indexation of pension amounts, and expansion of beneficiary coverage to sustain its impact.

Scheme Coverage

From FY 2021–22 onwards, the Ministry of Rural Development has made separate budgetary

provisions for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) from FY 2021-22 under the National

Social Assistance Programme (NSAP). In FY 2023–24, an amount of ₹1,733.19 crore was released for

SC beneficiaries and ₹1,003.20 crore for ST beneficiaries (as on 31 March 2024). Similarly, in FY 2024-

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
25, up to 31 December 2024, ₹1,386.98 crore and ₹730.58 crore have been released for SC and ST

beneficiaries respectively.

Proportion of SC beneficiaries has remained consistent at around 19%, while ST beneficiaries account

for about 10% of the total NSAP coverage from FY 2021–22 to FY 2024–25. This steady representation

aligns closely with the national demographic share of these groups (SCs: 16.6%, STs: 8.6% as per

Census 2011), indicating equitable inclusion in programme coverage. The stable year-on-year increase

in absolute numbers of SC and ST beneficiaries also reflects sustained outreach and effective targeting

of vulnerable social groups. However, to maintain inclusiveness, continued monitoring of beneficiary

identification and fund utilization is necessary to ensure timely disbursement and equitable benefit

adequacy across states. The focus should move beyond numeric inclusion to equity in adequacy

ensuring SC/ST beneficiaries, who often face multidimensional poverty, receive timely and sufficient

payments without procedural delays.

1.2 RATIONALE OF THE STUDY

NSAP has made significant financial outlays, and is vital for strengthening the social protection

system in the country. In 2023, an All-India performance audit of the NSAP was undertaken by CAG,

which reflected that although centrally financed, the NSAP’s implementation and the amount

of benefits, as well as its impact, varies from state to state. The report revealed several

irregularities and lapses in the planning, financial management, implementation, and

monitoring of the welfare scheme NSAP. It highlighted that as the scheme is being implemented

in demand-driven mode, there are chances that many of the eligible beneficiaries are left-out of the

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
coverage of scheme. On the other hand, it was also noted that many of the ineligible

beneficiaries were also drawing benefits from the scheme owing to deficiencies in the

verification mechanism, maintenance of requisite data and authentication systems. The

evaluation also highlighted lapses in payment mechanism including untimely and irregular

payments as well as the system being non-DBT compliant in some states. Based on their observations,

the CAG offered multiple recommendations to improve the performance of the scheme.

Regular independent evaluation of the scheme at this juncture therefore assumes great importance

to assess the status of scheme performance and identify the key enablers and barriers

influencing scheme implementation. It is also important from the perspective of vitality of

the scheme to help meet the sustainable development goals which is a prime agenda for the

Government. In view of the aforementioned factors, and with the objective of strengthening the

monitoring and evaluation systems for scheme implementation, AMS (Academy of Management

Studies) was commissioned by the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) through its Department of Rural

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
Development (DoRD) to conduct the “Impact Assessment & Evaluation of NSAP”.

The primary objective of the study was to assess the extent to which the National Social Assistance

implementation processes/road map for the continuation of the intervention.

➢ Improving the socio-economic status of the rural population

➢ Enabling the beneficiaries to actively participate in economic development

2 CHAPTER

Study Approach and Methodology

2.1 METHODOLOGICAL APPROACH

As illustrated in the figure alongside,

the assignment was undertaken in 3

phases. In the first phase, in close

consultation with the project

officials of the department of rural

development, the study design and

work plan was finalized. Then the

study/ data collection tools that

were used to gather information for

benchmarking the indicators were

developed.

The finalized tools were then translated into the local language for each of the states and converted

into soft format on ODK platform for capturing the primary data in computer assisted personal

interviewing (CAPI) mode using handheld android tablets.

The identification, deployment and training of the field staff on the data collection tools was the final

activity under this phase. Orientation training was provided to our field teams on the data collection tools

and methodologies that they would be required to adopt for the primary survey. Immediately after the

orientation training, the field teams were deployed on the field for carrying out primary survey with the

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
targeted respondents. In the second phase, the activity for the collection of both qualitative and

quantitative information was undertaken. Data validation was an integral activity under this phase and

was undertaken along with the data collection. Quality checks were carried out to detect any errors or

gaps. In the third & final phase, of the assignment, the analysis of the data was undertaken after

translating the enumerated data into English. Based on the information collected, the datasets were duly

collated and analyzed to develop the required indicators and the findings were accordingly documented

into a draft report. After incorporating the feedbacks from the client in the draft report, the agency shall

submit the final report for the study to the client. Subsequently, a PowerPoint Presentation will be made

for presenting and sharing the findings.

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
2.2 STUDY DESIGN AND EVALUATION APPROACH

A cross-sectional study design was adopted to assess the extent to which the programme has

achieved its objectives and to identify the key enablers and barriers that influence the

implementation processes. The planned design helped generate reliable measures of the

changes that can be attributable to the project.

Additionally, a mixed methods approach for data collection was adopted. Both primary and

secondary data were collected for the purpose of this study through appropriate quantitative

finalized after pre-testing and discussions with the DoRD officials.

3 CHAPTER

Scheme Implementation

3.1 ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE SCHEME

Launched in 1995, the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) has emerged as one of India’s

largest and longest-running social protection frameworks, fulfilling the constitutional vision under

Article 41 to support citizens facing old age, widowhood, disability, or the loss of a breadwinner. Over

nearly three decades, NSAP has grown into a nationwide safety net covering nearly 3 crore

beneficiaries. Its expansion, institutionalization, and direct impact on improving the quality of life

among the poorest households make NSAP one of the most significant pillars of India’s social

protection ecosystem.

1. Strengthening Household Security and Reducing
Financial Vulnerability
• 75.1% of beneficiaries reported that the pension
somewhat reduced their dependence on other
earning members in their household; 16.5% said
it significantly reduced dependence.

• States with higher top-ups like Andhra Pradesh,
Telangana, and Haryana, showed stronger
improvements in household stability and
income security, demonstrating the stabilizing
role of NSAP in low-income households.

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
• The scheme provides predictable, regular
support for elderly persons, widows, and
persons with disabilities who are traditionally
excluded from the labour market.

2. Improvements in Socio-Economic Well-Being
• 81-84% beneficiaries use pensions primarily for food and medicine.

• 63% reported improved food access, 68% improved ability to purchase personal essentials,
and 65% improved medical access.

• Nearly half the respondents borrow less for subsistence, indicating reduced distress
borrowing and better resilience.

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
• Strongest improvements recorded in Jammu & Kashmir, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu, where
70-90% of respondents reported positive changes across key well-being indicators.

3. Enhancing Dignity, Social Acceptance, and Self-Worth

• 67-68% beneficiaries reported improved treatment and respect within their families and
communities.

• Elderly persons, widows, and persons with disabilities noted greater social acceptance,
enhanced independence, and a renewed sense of self-worth.

• These findings resonate with global evidence showing that predictable social pensions
enhance dignity and strengthen social roles for older persons.

4. Improved Transparency Through DBT and Digital Systems

• 97% of beneficiaries have Aadhaar-linked bank accounts.

• Doorstep payments in states like Haryana and Andhra Pradesh ensure safe access for
immobile beneficiaries.

• The NSAP-PPS system digitizes beneficiary records and disbursement histories, improving
monitoring, reducing leakages, and strengthening programme governance.

5. Progress in Timely Disbursement and Beneficiary Convenience

• States such as Andhra Pradesh and Haryana consistently ensure timely and predictable
payments.

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
• Doorstep delivery, mobile banking, and simplified procedures have reduced travel time and
transaction burdens.

• 73% of beneficiaries expressed satisfaction with the overall scheme process, an
improvement over previous years when delays were widespread.

“After receiving the pension, we feel more independent because we can spend the money
according to our own wishes. Our family members treat us better now, and our access to
food and medicines has improved. We are able to meet our basic needs, which was not
possible earlier. We are satisfied with the overall process—from selection and sanction to
the disbursement of the pension. We feel a change in our confidence and self-esteems”
-Focus Group Discussions with Beneficiaries, Jammu & Kashmir

For nearly 30 years, the National Social Assistance Programme has anchored India’s commitment to

social justice, poverty alleviation, and dignity for vulnerable citizens. It has strengthened household

stability, reduced dependence and vulnerability, improved consumption, food security, and medical

access, enhanced dignity and social acceptance, expanded coverage to millions, improved

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
transparency through DBT and built a foundation for future social protection reforms. NSAP stands

today not only as a safety net, but as a central pillar of India’s social protection system that continues

to evolve, adapt, and uphold the constitutional promise of dignity and security for all.

3.4.2 Identification of Beneficiaries

Beneficiary identification processes vary significantly across states, reflecting differences in local

implementation practices. Overall, Gram Sabha meetings (36.3%) and panchayat officials (33.5%) were

the most common means of identifying beneficiaries, indicating the crucial role of local governance

institutions in the identification and selection process. States like Bihar (66.5%), Chhattisgarh (55.5%),

and Haryana (52%) relied heavily on the Gram Sabha, reflecting participatory approaches. In contrast,

Andhra Pradesh (63.8%), Telangana (56.7%), and Assam (54.3%) primarily depended on panchayat

ministry_department: Ministry of Rural Development
text:
officials. Jammu & Kashmir stood out, with 99.8% of beneficiaries reporting self-application, indicating

limited institutional involvement in identification. Identification through door-to-door surveys (3.1%)

and community or SHG involvement (0.43%) was minimal, highlighting underutilization of proactive

outreach methods. Some beneficiaries were also identified through ‘other’ local functionaries, such as

the Village Administrative Officer and the Village Assistant.

Overall, while community-based and official identification remain dominant, there is a need to

strengthen inclusive and participatory mechanisms, particularly in states where self-identification

dominates or community outreach is limited.
